items.stem: A quadrilateral with exactly one pair of parallel sides is called a ______.
items.markingKey: Trapezium.

items.stem: In one line: why is every square a rhombus, but not every rhombus a square?
items.answer: Both have four equal sides; a square additionally needs four right angles.
items.markingKey: Both have four equal sides; a square additionally needs four right angles.

items.stem: A kite has two pairs of equal ADJACENT sides. Explain why a rhombus is a special kind of kite.
items.answer: In a rhombus all four sides are equal, so both pairs of adjacent sides are equal — it satisfies the kite condition.
items.markingKey: In a rhombus all four sides are equal, so both pairs of adjacent sides are equal — it satisfies the kite condition.

items.stem: Name the quadrilateral whose diagonals are equal and bisect each other at right angles.
items.markingKey: Square.

items.stem: A quadrilateral has sides 5, 5, 8, 8 cm with the equal sides adjacent; its diagonals are unequal and one bisects the other at 90°. Name it.
items.markingKey: Kite.

items.stem: Describe a quadrilateral whose diagonals bisect each other but are neither equal nor perpendicular. Name it and justify.
items.answer: A parallelogram (non-rectangle, non-rhombus): bisecting diagonals ⇒ parallelogram; not equal ⇒ not a rectangle; not perpendicular ⇒ not a rhombus.
items.markingKey: A parallelogram (non-rectangle, non-rhombus): bisecting diagonals ⇒ parallelogram; not equal ⇒ not a rectangle; not perpendicular ⇒ not a rhombus.

items.stem:
Assertion (A): Every square is a rhombus.
Reason (R): A rhombus has four equal sides, and a square has four equal sides.
Choose the correct option.
items.answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
items.markingKey: (a) R gives the defining property shared.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

items.stem: Name the quadrilateral whose diagonals are equal and bisect each other, but are not perpendicular.
items.markingKey: (c) Rectangle.

items.stem: In one line: why is every rectangle a parallelogram, but not every parallelogram a rectangle?
items.answer: a rectangle has both pairs of opposite sides parallel; a parallelogram need not have right angles
items.markingKey: Shared property named (1 mark) and the extra condition the rectangle needs (1 mark).

items.stem: A quadrilateral has sides 7, 7, 10, 10 cm with the equal sides adjacent; its diagonals are unequal and one bisects the other at right angles. Name it.
items.markingKey: Two pairs of equal adjacent sides with perpendicular diagonals: kite.

items.stem: A quadrilateral with exactly one pair of parallel sides is called a …
items.markingKey: (c) Definition of a trapezium.

items.stem: Draw a family tree (or Venn diagram) showing how square, rectangle, rhombus, parallelogram, trapezium and kite are related. Use it to decide: is a square a kite? Justify.
items.answer: Yes, a square is a kite.
items.markingKey: Diagram with square inside rectangle and rhombus, both inside parallelogram (2 marks). A square has two pairs of equal adjacent sides, so it is a kite (1 mark).

items.stem: Plot A(0, 0), B(2, 0), C(3, 2) and D(1, 2). Name the quadrilateral ABCD and justify using side lengths or parallel sides.
items.markingKey: AB and DC are horizontal of length 2; AD and BC have the same slope; opposite sides parallel → parallelogram. AD = √(5) ≠ AB.

items.stem: What is the sum of the interior angles of (i) a quadrilateral, (ii) a hexagon?
Using one diagonal, explain in one line why the angle sum of a quadrilateral is 360°.
items.answer: A diagonal splits it into two triangles, each with angle sum 180°.
items.markingKey: A diagonal splits it into two triangles, each with angle sum 180°.

items.stem: Why is the sum of the exterior angles of ANY polygon 360°, regardless of the number of sides?
items.answer: Walking around the polygon you turn through each exterior angle and end up facing the same way, i.e. one full turn = 360°.
items.markingKey: Walking around the polygon you turn through each exterior angle and end up facing the same way, i.e. one full turn = 360°.

items.stem: The angles of a quadrilateral are 80°, 95°, 100° and x. Find x.
Each exterior angle of a regular polygon is 24°. How many sides does it have?
The angles of a quadrilateral are in the ratio 2 : 3 : 4 : 6. Find them. Can this quadrilateral be a trapezium (a pair of co-interior angles adding to 180°)?
items.answer: Angles 48°, 72°, 96°, 144°. No two of them add to 180°, so it cannot be a trapezium in any arrangement.
items.markingKey: Angles 48°, 72°, 96°, 144°. No two of them add to 180°, so it cannot be a trapezium in any arrangement.

items.stem: Find the measure of each interior angle of a regular polygon with 8 sides.
Nikhil cuts a quadrilateral tile with angles 71°, 101°, 109° and x°. Find x and say whether the tile could be a parallelogram.
items.answer: x = 79°; not a parallelogram (opposite angles not equal)
items.markingKey: x = 360 − 71 − 101 − 109 = 79°. A parallelogram needs both pairs of opposite angles equal.

items.stem: What is the sum of the interior angles of a nonagon?
Why is the sum of the exterior angles of ANY convex polygon 360°, whatever the number of sides?
items.answer: Walking once around the polygon you turn through each exterior angle and finish facing the start direction: one full turn.
items.markingKey: Full-turn argument, or n × 180° − (n − 2) × 180° = 360°.

items.stem:
Assertion (A): Each exterior angle of a regular hexagon is 60°.
Reason (R): The exterior angles of any polygon add up to 360°.
Choose the correct option.
items.answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

items.stem: Explain, using triangles, why the interior angles of a pentagon add up to 540°.
items.answer: A diagonal (or diagonals from one vertex) splits it into triangles, each with angle sum 180°.
items.markingKey: Number of triangles × 180°.

items.stem: Each exterior angle of a regular polygon is 30°. How many sides does it have?
items.markingKey: Exterior angles sum to 360°: 360 ÷ 30 = 12.

items.stem: State one diagonal property that a rectangle has but a general parallelogram does not.
items.answer: Its diagonals are equal in length.
items.markingKey: Its diagonals are equal in length.

items.stem: In one line: why are opposite angles of a parallelogram equal?
items.answer: Each pair of adjacent angles adds to 180° (co-interior angles), so angles opposite each other are both supplements of the same angle.
items.markingKey: Each pair of adjacent angles adds to 180° (co-interior angles), so angles opposite each other are both supplements of the same angle.

items.stem: A student says 'a quadrilateral with equal diagonals must be a rectangle.' Give a counter-example.
items.answer: An isosceles trapezium has equal diagonals but is not a rectangle.
items.markingKey: An isosceles trapezium has equal diagonals but is not a rectangle.

items.stem: In parallelogram ABCD, ∠A = 70°. Find ∠B, ∠C and ∠D.
The diagonals of a rhombus are 12 cm and 16 cm. Find its side.
items.markingKey: Half-diagonals 6 and 8 → side = √(36 + 64) = 10 cm.

items.stem: Two adjacent angles of a parallelogram are (3x + 10)° and (2x + 20)°. Find all four angles.
Diagonals of parallelogram PQRS meet at O. PO = 3y − 1 and OR = y + 5. Find y and the length PR.
items.answer: Diagonals bisect: 3y − 1 = y + 5 → y = 3; PO = 8, PR = 16.
items.markingKey: Diagonals bisect: 3y − 1 = y + 5 → y = 3; PO = 8, PR = 16.

items.stem: In rectangle ABCD the diagonals meet at O and ∠AOB = 60°. Show that triangle AOB is equilateral and find ∠OAD.
items.answer: OA = OB (halves of equal diagonals) and the vertex angle is 60°, so the base angles are 60° each → equilateral. ∠OAB = 60°, so ∠OAD = 90° − 60° = 30°.
items.markingKey: OA = OB (halves of equal diagonals) and the vertex angle is 60°, so the base angles are 60° each → equilateral. ∠OAB = 60°, so ∠OAD = 90° − 60° = 30°.

items.stem: In parallelogram ABCD, ∠A = 60°. The bisectors of ∠A and ∠B meet at P. Find ∠APB and explain why the answer does not depend on ∠A.
items.markingKey: ∠A + ∠B = 180°, so half of each adds to 90°; in triangle APB, ∠APB = 180° − 90° = 90°.

items.stem: In parallelogram ABCD, ∠A = 120°. The bisectors of ∠A and ∠B meet at P. Find ∠APB and explain why the answer does not depend on ∠A.
items.markingKey: ∠A + ∠B = 180°, so half of each adds to 90°; in triangle APB, ∠APB = 180° − 90° = 90°.

items.stem: In parallelogram ABCD, ∠A = 70°. The bisectors of ∠A and ∠B meet at P. Find ∠APB and explain why the answer does not depend on ∠A.
items.markingKey: ∠A + ∠B = 180°, so half of each adds to 90°; in triangle APB, ∠APB = 180° − 90° = 90°.

items.stem: The diagonals of a rhombus are 16 cm and 30 cm. Find the length of each side.
items.markingKey: Diagonals bisect at right angles: side = √(8² + 15²) = 17 cm.

items.stem: In parallelogram ABCD, ∠A = 80°. The bisectors of ∠A and ∠B meet at P. Find ∠APB and explain why the answer does not depend on ∠A.
items.markingKey: ∠A + ∠B = 180°, so half of each adds to 90°; in triangle APB, ∠APB = 180° − 90° = 90°.

items.stem: In one line: why are the opposite angles of a parallelogram equal?
items.answer: Adjacent angles are co-interior angles between parallel lines, so each pair adds to 180°; two angles supplementary to the same angle are equal.
items.markingKey: Uses co-interior angles (1 mark) and the conclusion (1 mark).

items.stem: In parallelogram PQRS, ∠P = (4x + 27)° and ∠R = (2x + 79)°. Find x and all four angles.
items.markingKey: Opposite angles equal: 4x + 27 = 2x + 79 → x = 26; adjacent = 180 − 131.

items.stem: In parallelogram ABCD, ∠A = 100°. The bisectors of ∠A and ∠B meet at P. Find ∠APB and explain why the answer does not depend on ∠A.
items.markingKey: ∠A + ∠B = 180°, so half of each adds to 90°; in triangle APB, ∠APB = 180° − 90° = 90°.

items.stem: Aryan uses 38 cm of ribbon to border a parallelogram-shaped card exactly once. One side is 12 cm. Find the other sides.
items.markingKey: Opposite sides equal: 2(12 + x) = 38 → x = 7.

items.stem: One angle of a parallelogram is 56°. Find the other three angles.
items.markingKey: Adjacent angles are supplementary: 180 − 56 = 124; opposite angles are equal.

items.stem: What is the minimum number of independent measurements needed to construct a unique quadrilateral?
items.markingKey: Five.

items.stem: In one line: why can't a quadrilateral be constructed uniquely from its four sides alone?
items.answer: Four hinged sides can flex into many shapes; a diagonal or an angle is needed to fix it.
items.markingKey: Four hinged sides can flex into many shapes; a diagonal or an angle is needed to fix it.

items.stem: Can you construct quadrilateral ABCD with AB = 3 cm, BC = 4 cm and diagonal AC = 10 cm? Explain.
items.answer: No: in triangle ABC, 3 + 4 < 10 violates the triangle inequality.
items.markingKey: No: in triangle ABC, 3 + 4 < 10 violates the triangle inequality.

items.stem: Outline the steps to construct ABCD with AB = 4 cm, BC = 5 cm, CD = 6 cm, DA = 4.5 cm, AC = 7 cm.
items.answer: Draw triangle ABC (AB = 4, BC = 5, AC = 7); from A cut an arc of 4.5 cm and from C an arc of 6 cm; their intersection is D; join AD, CD.
items.markingKey: Draw triangle ABC (AB = 4, BC = 5, AC = 7); from A cut an arc of 4.5 cm and from C an arc of 6 cm; their intersection is D; join AD, CD.

items.stem: Describe how to construct a rhombus with diagonals 6 cm and 8 cm.
items.answer: Draw AC = 8 cm, construct its perpendicular bisector, mark B and D 3 cm on either side of the midpoint, join. (Side comes out as 5 cm.)
items.markingKey: Draw AC = 8 cm, construct its perpendicular bisector, mark B and D 3 cm on either side of the midpoint, join. (Side comes out as 5 cm.)

items.stem: Which data sets give a UNIQUE quadrilateral? (i) 4 sides + 1 angle (ii) 3 sides + 2 included angles (iii) 2 adjacent sides + 3 angles (iv) 4 angles + 1 side.
items.answer: (i), (ii) and (iii) yes. (iv) no — the same angles with one side fixed still allow different shapes (only one side is fixed, the others can vary).
items.markingKey: (i), (ii) and (iii) yes. (iv) no — the same angles with one side fixed still allow different shapes (only one side is fixed, the others can vary).

items.stem: Can a quadrilateral ABCD be constructed with AB = 3 cm, BC = 5 cm and diagonal AC = 10 cm? Explain.
items.markingKey: (d) Triangle ABC would need AB + BC > AC, but 3 + 5 = 8 < 10.
options: Only if ABCD is a square

items.stem: Only two or three measurements are given for a rhombus: side 5 cm and one diagonal 8 cm. Explain why these are enough to construct it.
items.answer: The rhombus's own properties supply the other measurements.
items.markingKey: e.g. equal sides / right angles / bisecting diagonals of a rhombus fill in the missing data.

items.stem: Write the steps of construction for quadrilateral ABCD with AB = 4 cm, BC = 7 cm, CD = 6 cm, DA = 4 cm and AC = 9 cm.
items.answer: Draw triangle ABC from three sides, then triangle ACD on the other side of AC; join.
items.markingKey: Construct ΔABC (AB = 4, BC = 7, AC = 9); with centre C radius 6 and centre A radius DA cut arcs on the other side of AC to get D; join CD and DA.

items.stem:
Assertion (A): A square can be constructed if only the length of its diagonal is known.
Reason (R): The diagonals of a square are equal and bisect each other at right angles.
Choose the correct option.
items.answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
items.markingKey: (a) Draw the two equal perpendicular bisecting diagonals and join their ends.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

items.stem: To construct quadrilateral PQRS you are given PQ = 7 cm, ∠P = 75°, ∠Q = 105°, ∠R = 120°. What extra measurement is needed, and what kind of quadrilateral is formed if PS ∥ QR?
items.answer: One more side, e.g. QR; trapezium
items.markingKey: ∠P + ∠Q = 180° shows PS ∥ QR is consistent: trapezium. Five independent measurements are needed.

items.stem: A carpenter wants a rectangular frame 6 dm by 3 dm. He measures the four sides correctly but the frame still looks slanted. (i) Why can the frame still be slanted? (ii) What single measurement should he check, and what should it read? (iii) Name the property of rectangles this uses.
items.answer: (i) four sides do not fix the angles (ii) a diagonal, √(6² + 3²) ≈ 6.7 dm (iii) diagonals of a rectangle are equal
items.markingKey: 1 + 2 + 1 marks.

items.stem: Only two or three measurements are given for a rectangle: sides 5 cm and 3 cm. Explain why these are enough to construct it.
items.answer: The rectangle's own properties supply the other measurements.
items.markingKey: e.g. equal sides / right angles / bisecting diagonals of a rectangle fill in the missing data.

items.stem: Explain why four side lengths alone are not enough to construct a unique quadrilateral.
items.answer: A quadrilateral with fixed sides can flex (e.g. a square can be pushed into a rhombus); a diagonal or angle fixes it.
items.markingKey: Flexing argument or two different shapes with the same four sides.

items.stem: What is the minimum number of independent measurements needed to construct a unique quadrilateral?
items.markingKey: (a) Four sides alone do not fix the shape; a fifth measurement (e.g. a diagonal) is needed.
